items.title: Evolution of Planning & the Planning Commission
items.body:
## Pre-independence roots

Organised planning ideas predate 1947:

| Plan | Year | Proposer |
|---|---|---|
| Visvesvaraya Plan | 1934 | M. Visvesvaraya (*Planned Economy for India*) |
| National Planning Committee | 1938 | S.C. Bose; chaired by Nehru |
| Bombay Plan | 1944 | J.R.D. Tata, G.D. Birla & industrialists |
| Gandhian Plan | 1944 | S.N. Agarwal |
| People's Plan | 1945 | M.N. Roy |

Early thinkers Dadabhai Naoroji and M. Visvesvaraya shaped the idea of an organised, self-sustaining economy.

## The Planning Commission (1950)

- Set up by an **executive resolution of the Government of India in 1950** — a **non-statutory, non-constitutional** body.
- **Prime Minister** was ex-officio **Chairperson**; a full-time Deputy Chairman ran it.
- Task: frame **Five-Year Plans**, set national priorities, **allocate central funds** to states/sectors, and monitor progress.
- Followed a **centralised, top-down, socialist-influenced** model (Soviet inspiration) with the **public sector** as the main growth driver.

## Objectives & approaches

- Core objectives: **growth, equity/social justice, modernisation, self-reliance**.
- Post-1991 shift from **centralised to indicative planning** (state as facilitator).
- **73rd & 74th Amendments** enabled **decentralised planning** through PRIs and urban local bodies.

## National Development Council (NDC)

- Set up in **1952** by executive resolution (non-statutory); chaired by the **Prime Minister**, with all **Chief Ministers, Union Cabinet Ministers and Planning Commission members**.
- It was the **apex body that reviewed and approved every Five-Year Plan** before implementation. Along with **Parliament**, the NDC is the body most closely associated with 'planning' in India — the **Finance Commission and line ministries (Rural/Urban Development) are NOT**.
keyPoints: Planning Commission was set up in 1950 by an executive resolution — non-statutory and non-constitutional, chaired by the PM.
National Development Council (NDC, 1952): PM-chaired, includes all CMs; the apex body that approved the Five-Year Plans. NDC and Parliament are associated with planning, not the Finance Commission.
Pre-independence plans: Visvesvaraya Plan (1934), NPC (1938, Bose/Nehru), Bombay Plan (1944, Tata & Birla), People's Plan (1945, M.N. Roy).
Four objectives of Indian planning: growth, equity, modernisation and self-reliance.
India shifted from centralised planning to indicative planning after the 1991 reforms.
73rd and 74th Constitutional Amendments promoted decentralised planning via local bodies.

items.title: The Five-Year Plans (1951-2017) at a glance
items.body:
## Models & milestones

| Plan | Period | Model / Theme | Note |
|---|---|---|---|
| First | 1951-56 | Harrod-Domar; agriculture, irrigation | Bhakra-Nangal, Hirakud, IIT Kharagpur; **target exceeded** (3.6% vs 2.1%) |
| Second | 1956-61 | Mahalanobis; heavy industry | Bhilai/Rourkela/Durgapur steel plants; PSU-led |
| Third | 1961-66 | Gadgil-Yojana; self-reliance | **Failed** (wars 1962/65, drought) → Plan Holiday |
| Plan Holiday | 1966-69 | Annual plans | Food security; sowed the Green Revolution |
| Fourth | 1969-74 | Green Revolution, self-reliance | HYV seeds; hit by poor monsoons & 1971 war |
| Fifth | 1974-78 | 'Garibi Hatao' | Minimum Needs Programme; cut short in 1978 |
| Rolling Plan | 1978-80 | Flexible annual revision | Janata government; later abandoned |
| Sixth | 1980-85 | Poverty, employment, infra | Family planning; met target |
| Seventh | 1985-90 | Productivity, employment | 6.0% growth; IT sector begins |
| Annual Plans | 1990-92 | Crisis stabilisation | **1991 LPG reforms** launched |
| Eighth | 1992-97 | LPG era, private sector | 6.8% growth (highest so far) |
| Ninth | 1997-2002 | Growth with social justice | 5.4% vs 6.5% target |
| Tenth | 2002-07 | 8% growth target | 7.3% achieved |
| Eleventh | 2007-12 | Faster & inclusive growth | Global financial crisis |
| Twelfth | 2012-17 | 'Faster, Sustainable and More Inclusive Growth' | **Last Five-Year Plan** |

## Growth models to remember

- **Harrod-Domar** (First): growth driven by saving & investment rate.
- **Mahalanobis** (Second): heavy capital-goods industries for long-run growth.
- **Gadgil-Yojana** (Third): decentralised balanced regional development.
keyPoints: First Plan (1951-56): Harrod-Domar model, agriculture focus, exceeded target at 3.6%.
Second Plan (1956-61): Mahalanobis model, heavy industry, set up Bhilai/Rourkela/Durgapur steel plants.
Third Plan (1961-66): Gadgil-Yojana; failed due to Indo-China (1962) and Indo-Pak (1965) wars and drought.
Plan Holiday (1966-69): three annual plans replaced the regular plan.
Fifth Plan (1974-78) used the 'Garibi Hatao' slogan and Minimum Needs Programme.
Eighth Plan (1992-97) coincided with LPG reforms; Twelfth Plan (2012-17) was the last Five-Year Plan.
Twelfth Plan (2012-17) objective slogan: 'Faster, Sustainable and More Inclusive Growth'; Eleventh Plan: 'faster and more inclusive growth'.
items.mnemonic: Model order 'HMG' for first three plans = Harrod-Domar, Mahalanobis, Gadgil.

items.title: NITI Aayog — structure, role & federalism
items.body:
## From Commission to NITI Aayog

The Planning Commission was dissolved and **NITI Aayog (National Institution for Transforming India)** was created on **1 January 2015** by a **Union Cabinet resolution**, because the old top-down model no longer fit the **post-1991 liberalised, market-driven economy** (rigidity, over-centralisation, weak state consultation, limited private-sector role).

## Structure

- **Chairperson:** Prime Minister.
- **Governing Council:** all state Chief Ministers + UT Lt. Governors/administrators.
- **Vice-Chairman:** nominated by the PM (2026: **Ashok Lahiri**).
- **CEO:** senior civil servant (2026: **Anurag Jain**); plus full-time & part-time members and ex-officio members.

## Role vs the Planning Commission

| Aspect | Planning Commission | NITI Aayog |
|---|---|---|
| Nature | Fund-allocating planning body | Policy **think-tank / advisor** |
| Approach | Top-down, centralised | Bottom-up, **cooperative federalism** |
| Funds | Allocated funds to states | **No fund-allocation** role (now with **Finance Commission**) |
| Method | Five-Year Plans | 3-Year Action Agenda, 7-Year Strategy, 15-Year Vision |

## Key initiatives

- **Aspirational Districts Programme**, **SDG India Index**, **National Multidimensional Poverty Index (MPI)**, **Atal Innovation Mission** (Atal Tinkering Labs), **India Innovation Index**, **Composite Water Management Index**.
- Promotes **cooperative & competitive federalism** and data-driven, real-time monitoring.

## Viksit Bharat @2047

- NITI Aayog anchors the **Viksit Bharat @2047** vision — making India a **developed nation by 2047** (centenary of independence), covering economic growth, social progress, environmental sustainability and good governance.
keyPoints: NITI Aayog was established on 1 January 2015 by a Cabinet resolution as a policy think-tank; the PM is its Chairperson.
Governing Council comprises all state Chief Ministers; a Vice-Chairman and a CEO run it (2026: Ashok Lahiri and Anurag Jain).
Unlike the Planning Commission, NITI Aayog has no power to allocate funds — devolution now rests with the Finance Commission.
Bodies NOT part of NITI Aayog: the Finance Commission (constitutional, Art 280, fund devolution) and the FSDC (chaired by the Finance Minister, financial stability).
NITI Aayog replaced Five-Year Plans with a 3-Year Action Agenda, 7-Year Strategy and 15-Year Vision.
Flagship initiatives: Aspirational Districts Programme, SDG India Index, National MPI, Atal Innovation Mission.
Viksit Bharat @2047 is the vision to make India a developed nation by 2047, anchored by NITI Aayog.
items.mnemonic: NITI = No fund allocation, Idea (think-tank), Together with states (cooperative federalism), Innovation.

items.title: For Mains — Economic Planning & NITI Aayog
items.body:
A recurring **Paper-IV (Economy & Development)** theme — also usable in Paper-III governance questions — is whether India's move from directive planning to NITI Aayog's advisory model has served development. Build the answer across these dimensions.

| Dimension | Content to deploy |
|---|---|
| **Rationale for change** | Planning Commission's top-down, fund-allocating model mismatched the post-1991 market economy |
| **What changed** | Think-tank, no fund allocation (now Finance Commission), cooperative & competitive federalism |
| **Instruments** | 3-Year Action Agenda, 7-Year Strategy, 15-Year Vision; replaced Five-Year Plans |
| **Achievements** | Aspirational Districts, SDG India Index, National MPI, Atal Innovation Mission; data-driven governance |
| **Criticism** | No statutory status, no funds → limited leverage; 'advisory not transformative'; weak on employment |
| **Way forward** | Fiscal empowerment of states, outcome budgeting, Viksit Bharat @2047 |

**Data points & authorities to quote:** Planning Commission (1950, executive resolution) → NITI Aayog (**1 Jan 2015**); VC **Ashok Lahiri**, CEO **Anurag Jain** (2026); **15th Finance Commission** (Singh) handles devolution (41% vertical share); Twelfth Plan (2012-17) was the last; NITI's **SDG India Index** and **National MPI** feed competitive federalism; **Viksit Bharat @2047** vision. Thinkers/models: **Mahalanobis** (planning architect), **Harrod-Domar**, debates on 'cooperative federalism'.

**AP angle:** As a bifurcated, resource-constrained state, Andhra Pradesh benefits from NITI's cooperative-federalism and Aspirational Districts framework but has pressed for the special fiscal support promised under the AP Reorganisation Act 2014; AP's own planning (vision documents, Swarnandhra/development corporations) mirrors the national shift from plans to outcome-based strategy.

**Use in answers:** (1) frame as 'control → collaboration, allocation → facilitation'; (2) use a **two-column Planning Commission vs NITI Aayog table** as the body's spine; (3) cite the fund-allocation shift to the Finance Commission as the sharpest institutional change; (4) conclude that cooperative federalism must be matched by real fiscal empowerment of states.
keyPoints: Frame: rationale → what changed → instruments → achievements → criticism → way forward.
Key institutional shift: fund allocation moved from Planning Commission to the Finance Commission; NITI is advisory.
Quote NITI (1 Jan 2015), VC Ashok Lahiri, CEO Anurag Jain (2026); Twelfth Plan (2012-17) last; Viksit Bharat @2047.
Criticism: no statutory/fund power limits leverage; advisory not transformative.
AP angle: cooperative federalism + Aspirational Districts vs demand for Reorganisation-Act fiscal support.
